new_statements.quote: Las rallitas o asentos que pongo sobre de las vocales es para que se conosca en donde cae la fuerza de la pronunciación; y sí en un termino se ponen dos, es porque ambas son largas y con todo eso, esta lengua es mui violenta en su pronunciación. [Montoya 1789 apud Del Carpio-Penagos & Álvarez-Vázquez 2014: 215] || Accent is of the utmost importance in both these dialects ... The words for bird, snake and flower are the same; but Albornoz gives this very example to illustrate the importance of accent, nolō, a snake, nolô, a flower. Unfortunately, none of my authorities employ any accentual mark but the acute, and this appears to be syllabic. [Brinton 1886: 9]
new_statements.translation: The little strokes or accents that I put over the vowels are so that one may know where the force of the pronunciation falls; and if two are put on one word, it is because both [vowels] are long; and with all that, this language is very violent [forceful] in its pronunciation.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No placement rule is stated anywhere. The only first-hand statements are (a) Montoya 1789: prominence ('fuerza de la pronunciación') is marked word by word with an accent, implying it was not felt to be predictable; in his list the mark sits on the final syllable in roughly two thirds of accented forms (188/278), on the penult in 65 and antepenult in 21, the non-final cases largely being stem-final before the endings -mu/-me/-hu; (b) Albornoz (ca. 1690, via Adam 1887/Brinton 1886/Müller 1888): an 'acento largo' vs 'acento breve' contrast on the same (final) vowel distinguishes lexical pairs (nolō 'snake' / nolô 'flower'), singular vs plural and 1st vs 3rd person, read by Müller as final-vowel quantity, i.e. a length/tone-type contrast rather than stress position. Net: colonial orthographic evidence points to word-final (stem-final) prominence plus a quantity/tonal contrast, but no source formulates a stress rule.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing stated (Montoya's double accent marks = 'ambas son largas', i.e. two long vowels, not secondary stress).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; in Montoya's data forms ending in -mu, -me, -hu, -mo typically carry the accent on the preceding (stem-final) syllable (e.g. Cupúmu, Natúhmu, Charícame, Nitángame).
new_statements.domain_note: Citation forms in an elicited 1789 word list (isolated words, many with nominal n-/na- prefixes and -mu/-me endings); Albornoz's acento pairs are word-level lexical/morphological contrasts. Language extinct since late 19th/early 20th c; all evidence is philological.
new_statements.identity_note: All evidence is philological for extinct Chiapanec (chia1262, ISO cip) of Chiapa de Corzo/Suchiapa/Acala: Montoya's 1789 list was compiled at Chiapa (Chiapa de Corzo); Albornoz's Arte (ca. 1690) describes the same language. Brinton 1886 treats Chiapanec together with Mangue/Chorotega of Nicaragua (a separate Glottolog language), but the accent example he cites is Albornoz's Chiapanec.

new_statements.quote: i adviertase para maior claridad en los acentos de los vocablos q[ue] aqui se ofresieren ir escritos que con estas dos señales (—) (^) se distinguiran los que son en el acento largos o breves reparando en la | silaba sobre que va la dicha vocal i assi es [el] asento desta manera que si es largo lo denota esta señal (—) i si es breve lo denota esta (^) vg nacouī el muchacho, narîma la luz. i no es superflua esta advertensia pues ai tantos vocablos que tan solamente se distinguen en los acentos vg nolō largo la culebra. nolô breve la flor i el petate. que con el acento breve o largo se distingue el plural del singular vg nahuī largo la muger en singular. nahuî breve las mugeres en plur. [fol. 1r: Nota 1a q[ue] todos los vocablos desta lengua se terminan en letra vocal.]
new_statements.translation: And note, for greater clarity in the accents of the words that will appear written here, that with these two signs (—) (^) those that are long or short in accent will be distinguished, paying attention to the syllable over which the said vowel goes; and so the accent is this way: if it is long this sign (—) denotes it, and if it is short this one (^), e.g. nacouī 'the boy', narîma 'the light'. And this warning is not superfluous, since there are so many words that are distinguished only in their accents, e.g. nolō long 'the snake', nolô short 'the flower and the mat'; and by the short or long accent the plural is distinguished from the singular, e.g. nahuī long 'the woman' in the singular, nahuî short 'the women' in the plural. [fol. 1r: Note 1: all the words of this language end in a vowel.]

Fr. Juan de Albornoz'; IIIF manifest metadata: J…
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog rule for Chiapanec is empty and the one existing statement (Montoya 1789, apud Del Carpio-Penagos & Álvarez-Vázquez 2014 p. 215) reads the accent marks as 'donde cae la fuerza de la pronunciación' with no placement rule. Albornoz 1691, a century earlier and the primary grammar, likewise gives no placement rule but adds that his two diacritics encode long vs short 'acento' on a vowel (lexically and grammatically contrastive), with every example on the final vowel; compatible with Montoya's mostly-final accent marks (188/278 final in the earlier tally) but describes quantity rather than 'force'. It confirms first-hand what Adam 1887, Brinton 1886 and Müller 1888 report of Albornoz…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for which syllable is prominent. What Albornoz calls 'acento' is a two-way long (macron) vs short (circumflex) mark on a vowel, contrastive both lexically (nolō 'snake' vs nolô 'flower, mat') and grammatically (nahuī 'woman' vs nahuî 'women'); in every example the mark sits on the final vowel of the word, and all words end in a vowel (Nota 1a). This is a quantity (or quantity-plus-quality) contrast on a fixed vowel, not a statement of stress placement.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the only remarks are the lexical minimal pair nolō/nolô and the sg/pl pair nahuī/nahuî. A skim of the pronoun and verb chapters (views f12-f15, fols. 7v-11r) found no further accent remark beyond the same length mark used morphologically (Adam 1887 pp. 14-15 summarizes it as long accent = 1st person, short accent = 3rd person).
new_statements.identity_note: Albornoz describes the Chiapanec of Chiapa (de los Indios / de Corzo), Dominican province of San Vicente de Chiapas y Guatemala, 1691; the same variety Montoya 1789 recorded. Brinton 1886 applies Albornoz's nolo example to Mangue (Nicaragua) as well, but the manuscript itself is only about Chiapanec.

readall_conflicts: No source gives a stress-placement rule, so there is no placement disagreement. The two colonial witnesses use 'acento' for different things: Albornoz 1691 for a long/short vowel mark (macron vs circumflex) that distinguishes words and singular from plural, Montoya 1789 for 'where the force of pronunciation falls' (and doubled marks where 'both are long'). Both sets of marks fall predominantly on the final vowel, so they are compatible, but neither licenses a stress type beyond 'accent marks cluster on the final vowel; contrast is by quantity on that vowel'.
